pg006_n0004: This textbook, Music for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form Two students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0005: It is prepared in accordance with the 2023 Music Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I – IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg006_n0006: It is a revised edition of Music for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form Two that was published in 2023 in accordance with the 2005 syllabus issued by the then, Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg006_n0008: The book consists of seven (7) chapters, namely; Rhythm, Staff notation, Harmony, Musical terms and signs, The existence of musical sounds, Musical performances and Music production.
pg006_n0009: In addition to the contents, each chapter contains illustrations, activities and exercises.
pg006_n0010: You are encouraged to do all the activities, questions and exercises.
pg006_n0011: You are also required to prepare a portfolio for keeping records of the entire lessons.
pg006_n0012: This will enhance your understanding and development of the intended competencies for this level.
pg006_n0014: Additional learning resources are available in the TIE e-Library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or ol.tie.go.tz

pg007_n0007: Without precise rhythm, music lacks order, leaving nothing to dance to or nod along with.
pg007_n0008: While other elements like pitch, dynamics and harmony are essential, it is impossible to have music without rhythm.
pg007_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn several concepts related to rhythm, which include triplets, time signatures, and grouping of notes and rests.
pg007_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to read and write rhythmic patterns accurately and perform music in different meters.
pg007_n0018: When a note that is commonly divided into two equal parts is divided into three equal parts, the resulting group is known as a triplet.
pg007_n0019: For example, one semibreve can be divided into three equal parts of minims.
pg007_n0020: A minim can be divided into three equal parts of crotchets.
pg007_n0021: A crotchet can also be divided into three equal parts of quavers.
pg007_n0022: Table 1.1 shows how a beat that is usually divided into two is divided into three equal parts.
pg007_n0023: Note that, when forming a triplet, notes with flags like quavers, semiquavers and other smaller notes are beamed together, with the number “3” placed in the middle of the notes.
pg007_n0024: Notes without flags, like crotchets and minims, are grouped by a straight or curvy line with a “3” in the middle.

pg012_n0016: Time signatures in music are an essential part of rhythm helping musicians understand how beats are grouped in a piece.
pg012_n0017: They help to show the number of beats in each measure and which note gets one beat.
pg012_n0018: Understanding how time signatures affect the feel of a piece of music enables a musician to interpret and perform music effectively.
pg012_n0022: In simple time signatures, each beat can be divided into two equal parts.
pg012_n0023: These are called “simple” because each beat naturally divides into two, making them easy to count and play.
pg012_n0024: In this section, you will be introduced to simple time signatures (two-two, three-two, four-two and three-eight).
pg013_n0002: A two-two time signature: This can also be represented by a symbol known as alla breve or cut-time.
pg013_n0003: A two-two time signature means that there are two minims in a bar.
pg013_n0004: In a two-two time, the value of one beat is regarded as a minim.

pg018_n0019: Note grouping involves arranging or organising notes and/or rests according to the given time signature.
pg018_n0020: It involves beaming notes into groups or arranging the notes and rests correctly according to the time signature used.
pg018_n0021: Note grouping is important in music as it simplifies reading written music.
pg018_n0025: These are principles that guide musicians in grouping notes so the music is easier to read and play.
pg018_n0026: They depend on the time signature, which indicates how many beats are in each measure and how they are divided.
pg018_n0027: When notes are grouped correctly, it is easier to see where each beat is and how the rhythm flows.
pg018_n0028: This helps both the person writing the music and the person playing it to understand the music better.
pg018_n0029: The following are examples of rules to observe when grouping notes in music writing:
pg018_n0031: (a) Do not beam across a bar line: Beaming takes place within the measure.
pg018_n0032: If there is a note standing alone at the end of a measure, it should not be

pg019_n0014: (b) Do not beam across the centre of a measure:
pg019_n0015: In four-four time signatures, for example, the centre of the measure lies between the second and third beats.
pg019_n0016: These beats are always separated to ensure a clear rhythm for the reader.
pg019_n0017: Figure 1.31 shows how to avoid beaming across the centre of a measure.

pg019_n0028: (c) Observe the total number of semiquavers to be grouped:

pg023_n0015: Rules in grouping notes and rests
pg023_n0017: In music, notes and rests are grouped according to the time signature to create a clear and organised rhythmic structure.
pg023_n0018: The grouping helps performers understand the timing and emphasis of each beat within a measure.
pg023_n0019: However, there are some rules to be observed when applying grouping in measures that include notes and rests.
pg023_n0022: (a) Notes and rests should be grouped according to the division of a beat:
pg023_n0023: When rests are used in a bar, they have to represent the main beat according to the time signature used.

pg024_n0007: (b) A correct rest sign for a particular beat should be used:
pg024_n0008: When a rest sign is used in a bar, it should equivalently represent a particular beat to complete a bar.

pg024_n0026: (c) There should not be use of many rests to represent a beat:
pg024_n0027: Where possible, it is better to avoid using many rests to represent a beat.
pg024_n0028: Each rest used should represent a particular beat.

pg027_n0007: Staff notation can be regarded as the universal language of music, which makes it possible for musicians to communicate and perform music accurately across different cultures.
pg027_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn the use of the grand staff in music notation as well as the construction of various major and minor scales.
pg027_n0009: The competencies developed will enable you to compose music in different keys and perform music written in the grand staff.
pg027_n0013: A world without a written system for music
pg027_n0017: The grand staff, also known as the great staff, is a musical notation system that combines treble and bass staffs.
pg027_n0018: In the grand staff, the treble and bass staffs are joined by a vertical line at the beginning (left-hand side) while normally connected by a brace or bracket.
pg027_n0019: The grand staff is used to notate music for instruments such as piano, harp and voice.

pg033_n0010: In music, scales and key signatures are closely related since a key signature shows which notes in a scale are sharp or flat.
pg033_n0011: Each scale belongs to a certain key, and the key signature tells musicians which notes to play throughout a song.
pg033_n0012: For example, the G major scale has the notes G, A, B, C, D, E and F♯.
pg033_n0013: Therefore, its key signature has one sharp on note F (F♯).
pg033_n0014: This connection helps musicians to easily know which notes to play, hence making reading music easier.
pg033_n0018: Scale degree is the position of a particular note on a scale in relation to the tonic note.
pg033_n0019: A major scale has eight notes whereby the eighth note is a repetition of the first note (tonic) in a higher pitch.
pg033_n0020: Each of these eight notes has a degree at a particular scale.
pg033_n0021: Note that, to refer to a scale degree, an up-arrow symbol (^), called “caret” is normally placed before the numbers which indicate the note’s position in the scale.

pg034_n0050: Scale degrees are determined in relation to the tonic note.
pg034_n0051: For example, in the scale of the G major, the tonic note is G.
pg034_n0052: Therefore, the positions of other notes of the scale will be identified starting from note G.

pg034_n0075: The circle of fifths is a diagram that helps to understand keys and key signatures in music.
pg035_n0002: shows the number of sharps or flats in a particular key and the order in which they occur.
pg035_n0003: Moving clockwise around the circle of fifths adds the number of sharps to the key signature.
pg035_n0004: Moving anticlockwise around the circle of fifths adds the number of flats to the key signature.
pg035_n0005: Figure 2.15 shows the direction of sharps and flats on the circle of fifths.

pg035_n0009: Pitches are organised in a sequence of perfect fifths when moving clockwise on the circle of fifths.
pg035_n0010: A sequence of perfect fifths involves a distance of five notes in an interval of fifths (5 notes), for example, an interval from note C to G (C, D, E, F and G).
pg035_n0011: Pitches are organised starting from the key of C at the top of the circle.
pg035_n0012: Moving clockwise in a sequence of perfect fifths, the series is C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯, C♯ as shown in Figure 2.16.

pg035_n0017: A sequence of perfect fourths involves a distance of four notes in an interval of fourths (4 notes).
pg035_n0018: For example, an interval from note C to F (C, D, E,

pg036_n0013: The major scale is the basis for nearly all music you are familiar with.
pg036_n0014: Other scales are described based on their relationships to the major scale.
pg036_n0015: In this section, you will learn to construct the ‘A’, B♭ and E♭ major scales.
pg037_n0003: For example, a song created in the G major scale will be in the key of G major and will be written using the G major key signature.
pg037_n0007: When constructing the ‘A’ major scale, you can arrange a series of eight notes starting from the first note, which is ‘A’.
pg037_n0008: This can be done while following the pattern for constructing major scales, which is T-T-S-T-T-T-S.
pg037_n0009: The following are steps that can be followed when constructing the ‘A’ major scale:
pg037_n0013: Write a series of eight notes from note A.
pg037_n0017: Count the steps between the notes while following the pattern T-T-S-T-T-T-S as follows:
pg037_n0024: From note B to C = Semitone; however, since the pattern for major scales requires you to count the whole step or tone (T), you have to increase the distance between note B and C.
pg037_n0025: This can be done by raising note C using a sharp (♯) sign to get the whole step or tone.
pg037_n0026: Therefore, you will count from note B to C♯ = Tone (T).
pg037_n0029: From note C♯ to D = Semitone (S)
pg037_n0032: From note D to E = Tone (T)
pg037_n0035: From note E to F = Semitone; however, since the pattern for major scales requires you to count the whole step or tone (T), you have to increase the distance between note E and F.
pg037_n0036: This can be done by raising note F using a sharp (♯) sign to get the whole step or tone.
pg037_n0037: Therefore, you will count from note E to F♯ = Tone (T).

pg042_n0019: In most cases, music played in a major key becomes live and entertaining.
pg042_n0020: However, music that arouses a feeling of sadness is in a minor key.
pg042_n0021: Minor scales sound different from major scales because they are constructed on different patterns of intervals.
pg042_n0022: At this level, you will learn minor scales related to C, F and G major scales.
pg043_n0004: In music, every major key has a relative minor, and every minor key has a relative major.
pg043_n0005: A major key that shares the key signature with a minor key is a relative major of that particular minor key.
pg043_n0006: On the other hand, a minor key that shares the key signature with a major key is a relative minor of that particular major key.
pg043_n0007: Even though they have the same key signature, a minor scale and its relative major sound different.
pg043_n0008: A relative minor key always starts on the 6th degree or solfege la of the corresponding major scale.
pg043_n0009: Figure 2.29 shows how to identify a relative minor key in the C major scale by observing the 6th degree or solfege la of the scale.

pg045_n0058: Another way to identify the relative minor of the major key is to count three half steps down from the major key’s first note.
pg045_n0059: For example, if you start on G major, counting down three half steps leads to E minor, which is its relative minor.
pg045_n0060: The same works in vice versa: count three half steps up to find the relative major of a minor key.
pg045_n0062: Note that, in order to determine the key of a musical piece, you must look at its pitch content.
pg045_n0063: In particular, the last note should determine the name of its key.
pg045_n0064: Normally, a piece of music should end on a note that gives the name of its key or scale.
pg045_n0065: By looking at the final note or combination of notes in a piece, you should gain a clear idea of whether it is based on the major or the minor scale that is associated with its key signature.
pg045_n0066: For example, a melody in Figure 2.35 uses a key signature for G major but ends with note E.

pg046_n0014: There are three types of minor scales.
pg046_n0015: These are natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales.

pg055_n0007: Harmony plays an important role in shaping the mood and overall texture of a musical piece.
pg055_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn several aspects related to harmony, including intervals and tonic triads.
pg055_n0009: The competencies developed will enable you to identify and construct intervals and triads.
pg055_n0010: It will also enhance your ability to recognise musical sounds by ear and apply the skill in music creation.
pg055_n0014: Having isolated melodies only without blending sounds
pg055_n0018: In music theory, an interval is the distance between two pitches.
pg055_n0019: For instance, on a piano, it can be the distance from note C to D, C to G, D to A or any others.
pg055_n0020: Understanding intervals allows musicians to identify relationships between notes, compose music and analyse different compositions effectively.
pg055_n0021: When finding the interval between two notes, we normally count from the lower note to the upper one.
pg055_n0022: Figure 3.1 shows an interval between two notes from A to E on the staff and a piano keyboard.

pg056_n0004: Intervals can be constructed either harmonically or melodically.
pg056_n0005: A harmonic interval occurs when two notes are played or sung at the same time.
pg056_n0006: A melodic interval occurs when two notes are played or sung one after another or in succession.

pg056_n0019: This involves naming or recognising the distance between two pitches.
pg056_n0020: The identity of an interval can be determined by considering the quantity (numeric size) and quality of an interval.
pg056_n0021: At this level, however, you will only learn how to identify intervals by their quantities or numerical sizes.
pg056_n0023: Quantity or numeric size of intervals
pg056_n0025: The quantity of an interval is identified by counting the number of notes from the lowest to the highest note in a particular interval.
pg056_n0026: For example, to identify the interval from C to E, you have to count the number of notes in between these notes.
pg056_n0027: You will find that there are three notes (C, D and E) when you count from C to E.
pg056_n0028: Figure 3.4 shows how to count notes from note C to E on a staff.

pg057_n0004: Intervals can be simple or compound. At this level, you will learn simple intervals.
pg057_n0006: These are intervals found within an octave.

pg057_n0041: When two notes have the same pitch, they result in a unison or prime interval.
pg057_n0043: When two notes are an octave apart, they result in an octave (8ve) interval.
pg057_n0044: For example, from C to C makes a quantity (numeric size) of an octave (8ve), which is a distance of eight notes.

pg060_n0021: In music, a tonic triad is built on the first note of a scale which is also called the tonic note.
pg060_n0022: It is one of the most important triads in any key because it gives the music a sense of home or rest.
pg060_n0023: A tonic triad is like the musical “home base” that other triads move away from and return to.
pg060_n0024: Whether in major or minor keys, the tonic triad helps listeners feel where the music begins and ends.
pg060_n0025: Composers often begin and end musical pieces with the tonic triad to create a feeling of completeness.
pg061_im009: Activity 3.4: (a) Explore various music scores to identify the tonic triads used. (b) Listen to any musical piece to identify how a tonic triad begins and ends the piece.

pg061_n0007: Tonic triads are constructed from the first degree (^1), that is, ‘do’ in major keys and ‘la’ in minor keys.
pg061_n0008: For example, in ‘A’ major, the tonic triad includes ‘A’ as do (the first note), C♯ as mi (the third note) and E as so (the fifth note).

pg065_n0007: Different feelings are aroused in different parts of the music when musical terms and signs are used.
pg065_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn several musical terms and signs that indicate tempo, articulations and repetition.
pg065_n0009: The competencies developed will enable you to express various feelings in musical performances and compositions.
pg065_n0017: These are terms and signs that indicate the speed of music; that is, how fast or slow certain music should be performed.
pg065_n0018: Tempo can be indicated using Italian terms or with a specific number of beats per minute (BPM).
pg065_n0019: Musicians normally use a metronome to practise staying in tempo and maintaining a consistent rhythm.
pg065_n0020: A metronome is a device that produces a regular and steady beat at a set tempo.
pg065_n0021: However, there are digital metronomes that can be found as applications in digital devices, such as smartphones, tablets, laptops and so forth.
pg065_n0022: The following are examples of terms and signs that indicate tempo:
pg065_n0025: Rallentando (Rall): This is a term that indicates tempo changes.
pg065_n0026: Rallentando means that the tempo is gradually slowing down.
pg065_n0027: It is marked as Rall and placed above the staff.
pg065_n0028: Figure 4.1 shows an example of how rallentando is applied on a melody.
pg066_im003: Musical staff in 4/4 time labeled 'Rall,' showing a melody example for rallentando with notes progressing across the bar and ending with a final barline.
pg066_n0004: (b) Calando: This is a term that indicates changes in both tempo and volume.
pg066_n0006: Calando means that the tempo is gradually slowing down and the volume of the song is fading away or slowing down.
pg066_n0007: Calando is also placed above the staff as shown in Figure 4.2.
pg066_im004: Musical staff in 2/4 time with one sharp, labeled 'Callando,' showing a melody example with single notes and short beamed notes ending at a final barline.
pg066_n0011: (c) Vivace: This term indicates that a music piece is performed quickly, lively and energetically (120-168 BPM).
pg066_n0013: Vivace is placed either above the first measure to indicate the tempo or above the new section to indicate changes in tempo.
pg066_n0014: Figure 4.3 shows an example of how vivace is applied to a melody.
pg066_im005: Musical staff labeled 'Vivace' in 3/4 time with a three-sharp key signature, showing a lively melody with quarter notes, beamed notes, a rest, and a dotted final note.
pg066_n0018: (d) Presto: This is a term used to mean that a tempo is very fast (169-200 BPM).
pg066_n0020: Presto can be placed either above the first measure to indicate the tempo or above the new section to indicate changes in tempo.
pg066_n0021: Figure 4.4 shows an example of how presto is applied to a melody.
pg066_im006: Musical staff labeled 'Presto' in 3/4 time with one sharp, showing a fast melody of ascending and descending notes, including a dotted final note and closing barline.
pg066_n0025: (e) Largo: This is a term used for a very slow and broad tempo (40-60 BPM).
pg066_n0027: Largo can be placed either above the first measure to indicate the tempo or above the new section to indicate changes in tempo.
pg066_n0028: Figure 4.5 shows an example of how largo is applied to a melody.
pg067_im003: Melody in B-flat major and 3/4 time marked Largo, showing a slow example phrase across several measures.
pg067_n0004: (f) Grave: This is a term used for a very slow and solemn tempo (20-40 BPM).
pg067_n0005: Grave can be placed either above the first measure to indicate the tempo or above a new section to indicate changes in a tempo.
pg067_n0006: Figure 4.6 shows an example on of how grave is applied to a melody.
pg067_im004: Melody in B-flat major and 2/4 time marked Grave, with several triplet figures demonstrating a very slow, solemn tempo.

pg067_n0013: When a tempo mark is used, it indicates that a specific speed has to be observed when performing the music.

pg068_n0023: Articulation refers to how a specific note or pitch is performed.
pg068_n0024: The application of articulations depends on the instrument making the music.
pg068_n0025: For example, the technique used by a violin player to slur notes will be completely different from that of a trumpet player.
pg068_n0026: A pianist and a singer will also apply different cues to make a melody sound legato.
pg068_n0027: The following is a short list of some common articulations, their names, meaning and what they look like when notated.
pg068_n0029: (a) Tenuto: It refers to a situation of holding the musical note for its full value; thus, giving it a slight emphasis. The symbol for tenuto is a short line on the respective note, as shown in Figure 4.9.
pg068_im006: Musical staff in treble clef with three sharps and 3/4 time, showing a short melody with tenuto marks on several notes.

pg069_n0002: (b) Subito: This is a term that means ‘quickly or suddenly’.
pg069_n0003: It is used alongside other musical commands to make their effects immediate and sudden.
pg069_n0004: Some common examples of subito commands include the following:
pg069_n0007: (i) subito forzando or sforzando (sfz), which means suddenly with force
pg069_n0009: (ii) piano subito (p sub), which means suddenly soft
pg069_n0011: (iii) subito forte (sf), which means suddenly loud

pg069_n0028: When performing a piece of music, various sections may require repetition according to the music composer.
pg069_n0029: Repetition of parts of a musical piece is one of the basic principles of organising music during composition.
pg069_n0030: Various terms and signs are used to show repetition of just a section or a whole piece of music.
pg070_n0002: These are hereby explained and shown in figures 4.11 to 4.14.
pg070_n0004: (a) This is a sign which shows that the previous one bar should be repeated.

pg070_n0009: Sometimes, the sign is embedded with numerals to indicate the number of bars to be repeated.
pg070_n0010: For example, when ‘3’ is embedded in the sign, it means that the previous three bars should be repeated.

pg070_n0020: (c) Da Capo (D.C.): This is a term that means, “Repeat from the beginning.”
pg070_n0022: This term is normally used in long musical pieces, which may include other repetition signs.
pg070_n0023: When a composer needs performers to repeat a section or whole piece of music from the beginning, the term Da Capo (D.C.) is used, as shown in Figure 4.14.

pg073_n0007: Musical sounds fill our world every day.
pg073_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn various musical instruments and their classification based on how they produce sound.
pg073_n0009: You will also learn properties of musical sounds, sources of musical sounds and theories explaining the existence of musical sounds.
pg073_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to classify musical instruments based on how they produce sound, recognise sources and properties of musical sounds and use scientific ideas to describe how musical sounds exist.
pg073_n0014: Life filled with only non-musical sounds
pg073_n0017: Music is an essential part of human culture, and musical instruments are the tools that bring it to life.
pg073_n0018: They are tools used to create sound and express music.
pg073_n0019: There are various types of musical instruments in different shapes, sizes and materials.
pg073_n0020: Each instrument produces unique sounds based on how they are played.
pg073_n0021: Some instruments produce sound by plucking strings, others by blowing air and some by hitting the surface of an instrument.
pg073_n0024: Musical instruments can be studied in different aspects, including their classes or categories, how they are made, how they work, their history and their cultural importance.
pg073_n0025: The study that focuses on these aspects of musical instruments is
pg074_n0003: Organology is a crucial field that develops the understanding of musical instruments and their role in human culture.
pg074_n0004: By studying instruments from different time periods and regions, organology helps to understand how music has evolved and how instruments shape musical traditions across the world.
pg074_n0005: Generally, this field is important because it allows people to study and compare instruments from different cultures, helping to preserve and understand the history of music.
pg074_n0007: One of the most important aspects of organology is the classification of musical instruments.
pg074_n0008: The Hornbostel-Sachs system is one of the most widely used systems for classifying musical instruments.
pg074_n0009: It was developed in 1914 by two music scholars, Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs.
pg074_n0010: This system categorises instruments based on how they produce sound.
pg074_n0011: It is used all over the world to help people study and understand different musical instruments from various cultures.
pg074_n0012: According to the Hornbostel-Sachs system, there are five main groups of musical instruments, namely, idiophones, chordophones, aerophones, membranophones and electrophones.
pg074_n0016: These are musical instruments that produce sound when the whole body of an instrument vibrates after being struck, rubbed, scraped, plucked or shaken.
pg074_n0017: Due to their ways of producing sound, in some cases, these instruments are termed as percussions.
pg074_n0018: Triangles, bar chimes, maracas, cymbals and claves are examples of Western idiophones.
pg074_n0019: Manyanga, kayamba, chungu na kigoda, kinu na mchi (mortar and pestle), mbeta, njuga, marimba ya mkono (lamellaphone) and marimba ya vibao (xylophone) are examples of traditional Tanzanian idiophones.

pg076_n0011: These are also referred to as string instruments.
pg076_n0012: It is a group of musical instruments that produce sounds by bowing, hammering, plucking or strumming on the strings.
pg076_n0013: Examples of these instruments include a piano, which produces sound through vibrating strings that are struck by hammers.
pg076_n0014: The strings resonate within the piano’s body to produce sound.
pg076_n0015: Chordophones also include a family of violin instruments such as, a violin itself, viola, cello and double bass, which produce sound by pushing and pulling a bow over the strings (bowing), or by plucking strings.
pg076_n0016: Acoustic guitar is another example of chordophones that is played by plucking or strumming strings.
pg076_n0017: Oud and qanun are other examples of chordophones originating from the Arab societies.
pg076_n0018: Examples of traditional chordophones found in Tanzania are zeze, enanga, litungu, bango (ipangwa) and ndono.

pg078_n0002: Note that, according to the Hornbostel-Sachs system, the piano is classified as a chordophone.
pg078_n0003: However, some musicians and percussionists argue that the piano belongs to the percussion and not string family because the player presses keys rather than plucking or bowing strings.
pg078_n0004: Hence, its sound is initiated by hammers striking the strings.
pg078_n0005: This makes it similar to percussion instruments like the xylophone.
pg078_n0006: As a result of this debate, the piano is best considered a hybrid instrument.
pg078_n0007: That means it fits into categories of chordophones and percussions.

pg078_n0016: These are also referred to as wind instruments.
pg078_n0017: They are musical instruments that produce sound by vibrating a column of air.
pg078_n0018: Aerophones can further be grouped into brass and woodwind instruments.
pg078_n0019: Brass instruments are made of metal, particularly brass and create sound through the vibration of the player’s lips on the mouthpiece.
pg078_n0020: The air that passes through the player’s lips goes into the air column of the instrument and creates sound.
pg078_n0021: Examples of brass instruments are trumpets, trombones, tuba, horn and cornet.
pg078_n0022: Woodwind instruments create sound when a wooden reed attached to the instrument’s mouthpiece is blown to vibrate and produce sound.
pg078_n0023: Saxophones, clarinets and flutes are good examples of woodwind instruments.
pg078_n0024: Accordion is another example of a wind instrument.
pg078_n0025: It produces sound when the user expands or compresses the bellows while pressing the keys or the buttons.
pg078_n0026: The bellows cause air to flow across metal reeds and produce sound.
pg078_n0027: Baragumu (animal horn) is an example of common traditional aerophones found in Tanzania.
pg078_n0028: It is also known by various names in different societies in Tanzania.
pg078_n0029: For example, it is known as enzamba in Kagera, nhandala in Shinyanga, ndulele in Dodoma and ngarapi in Njombe.
pg078_n0030: Other traditional Tanzanian aerophones include lipenenga in Ruvuma and lilandi in Mara.

pg080_n0029: Different types of drums can be found in various societies.

pg083_n0015: Sound is a form of energy that travels as vibrations through air, water or solid objects.
pg083_n0016: Sound begins with the vibration of an object such as a table that is pounded or a string that is plucked.
pg083_n0017: The vibrations are transmitted to the ears by a medium, which is usually air.
pg083_n0018: As a result of the vibrations, the eardrums start vibrating too and signals are transmitted to the brain.
pg083_n0019: The brain then processes these signals by selecting, organising and interpreting them.
pg083_n0020: Sounds may be perceived as pleasant or unpleasant depending on their nature.

pg083_n0031: Music can be distinguished from other sounds by recognising the four main properties of musical sounds: pitch, dynamics, timbre (tone colour) and duration.
pg083_n0033: (a) Pitch: This refers to the highness or lowness we hear in a sound.
pg083_n0034: The faster the vibrations, the higher the pitch; the slower the vibrations, the lower the pitch.
pg083_n0035: In general, when the vibrating object is small, it vibrates faster, producing a higher pitch.
pg083_n0036: For example, a whistle has a high pitch, while a bass drum has a low pitch.
pg084_n0002: (b) Dynamics: This determines how strong a sound is.
pg084_n0003: It is the degree of loudness or softness in music.
pg084_n0004: Loudness is related to the amplitude of the vibrations that produces the sound, whereby larger vibrations result in louder sound.
pg084_n0005: For example, whispering is quieter while shouting is louder.
pg084_n0006: Another example is that the harder a piano key is pressed, the louder its sound.
pg084_n0007: A dynamic change happens when instruments are played more loudly or softly.
pg084_n0008: Such a change may be made either suddenly or gradually.
pg084_n0009: A gradual increase in loudness often creates excitement, particularly when the pitch rises too.
pg084_n0010: On the other hand, a gradual decrease in loudness can create a sense of calm.
pg084_n0012: (c) Timbre or tone colour: This refers to the unique tone of an instrument or voice.
pg084_n0013: For example, we can tell the difference between a piano and a guitar even when they are played in the same note at the same dynamic level.
pg084_n0014: The quality that distinguishes them is their tone colours (timbre).
pg084_n0015: Composers often create a melody with a particular tone colour of an instrument.
pg084_n0017: (d) Duration: It refers to how long or short a sound lasts.
pg084_n0018: In music, notes can be held for a short or long time.
pg084_n0019: For example, a piano key tapped quickly makes a short sound while a violin makes a long sound when bowed slowly.
pg084_n0020: Several factors can affect the duration of a sound.
pg084_n0024: (i) How an instrument is played; for example, a drummer can hit the drum quickly to create a short sound or let the sound ring for longer time.
pg084_n0026: (ii) The material of the object; for example, a metal bell rings longer than a wooden block.
pg084_n0028: (iii) The environment; for example, sounds produced in a big hall last longer because of echo and reverb.

pg085_n0024: Theories explaining the existence of musical sounds
pg085_n0026: Music is a universal language that has been part of human life for centuries.
pg085_n0027: The existence of musical sounds can be explained through multiple theories, each presenting a different view.
pg085_n0028: These theories work together to give us a complete understanding of why musical sounds exist and why music is such an important part of human life.
pg085_n0029: The following are examples of theories that explain the existence of musical sounds:
pg085_n0031: (a) The physical theory: This theory explains that musical sounds exist because of vibrations.
pg085_n0032: When an object vibrates, it creates sound waves that travel through air, water or solids until they reach the human ear.
pg085_n0033: For example, a vibrating guitar string pushes air molecules, producing sound waves.
pg085_n0034: The frequency of these vibrations determines the pitch of the sound.
pg085_n0035: Faster vibrations produce high-pitched sounds (such as a whistle), while slower vibrations create low-pitched sounds (such as a drum).
pg085_n0036: According to this theory, changing the shape, size or material of musical instruments can affect the sound they produce.
pg086_n0002: The shape controls how sound waves travel, influencing the tone.
pg086_n0003: For example, a trumpet’s narrow tube creates a bright sound, while a tuba’s wide shape produces a deep tone.
pg086_n0004: The size determines pitch, with larger instruments (such as a bass drum) producing lower pitches and smaller ones (such as a snare drum) creating higher pitches.
pg086_n0005: The material affects timbre or tone colour of an instrument, for example a wooden guitar compared to a metal trumpet.
pg086_n0008: This theory explains why different instruments sound unique, even when playing the same note.
pg086_n0009: According to the theory, every musical sound consists of a fundamental tone (the main pitch we hear) and overtones (extra frequencies that shape the sound).
pg086_n0010: These overtones create harmonics, which give each instrument a distinct timbre.
pg086_n0011: For example, a piano and a violin playing the same note will sound different because of their unique overtones.
pg086_n0012: The material and structure of an instrument influence how these harmonics are produced.
pg086_n0013: This theory helps explain why different musical instruments can be recognised instantly, even when they play the same melody.
pg086_n0016: This theory suggests that musical sounds follow mathematical patterns.
pg086_n0017: The Greek philosopher known as Pythagoras discovered that the length of a vibrating string determines its pitch.
pg086_n0018: For example, when a guitar string is cut in half, it produces a pitch one octave higher.
pg086_n0019: This theory is also considered when tuning instruments, particularly in Western music.
pg086_n0020: For example, by considering the mathematical relationships between tones, an octave is divided into 12 equal steps.
pg086_n0023: This theory explains that the human brain is wired to detect music.
pg086_n0024: Studies show that the brain processes musical sounds in a special way, different from other sounds.
pg086_n0025: It helps us recognise melodies, rhythms and harmonies, and some people even have perfect pitch, meaning they can identify musical notes without any reference from a musical instrument.
pg086_n0026: Studies also show that music affects emotions and memory.
pg086_n0027: For example, babies respond to lullabies, proving that musical sounds influence human emotions from birth.
pg086_n0028: Scientists have discovered that listening to music releases dopamine, a chemical that makes us feel happy.
pg086_n0029: This explains why people enjoy music, feel emotional connections to songs and use music for relaxation or motivation.
pg086_n0032: This theory states that music is influenced by society, history and traditions.
pg086_n0033: Different cultures have unique musical systems,
pg087_n0002: showing that music is not just natural but also a product of human creativity.
pg087_n0003: For example, in Western music, there are 12 tones in an octave.
pg087_n0004: In Indian and Arabic music, there are more than 12 tones.
pg087_n0005: Similarly, some societies focus on complex rhythms, while others focus on simple rhythms.
pg087_n0006: Music is also used in different cultural contexts, such as religious ceremonies, storytelling and social events.
pg087_n0007: Studies have shown that music reflects the values and history of a society.

pg089_n0018: Songwriting is the process of making a song by creating lyrics, melodies and musical structure for a song.
pg089_n0019: Songwriters put together different parts like verses, choruses and bridges to build a complete and interesting song.
pg089_n0020: People write songs for different purposes including personal expression, professional performance and others.
pg089_n0021: A well-written song not only sounds interesting but also tells a story, conveys emotions and connects deeply with listeners.
pg089_n0022: Songwriting has the power to move and inspire, leaving a lasting impact in peoples’ hearts and minds.
pg089_n0023: It is not just about words and tunes; it also needs good structure, smooth flow and real emotion to make the song special and unforgettable.

pg090_n0011: When writing a song for any purpose, it is important to understand the main elements that make a good song.
pg090_n0012: The following are the fundamental elements that contribute to the structure, feel and impact of a song:
pg090_n0017: Melody: This is the main tune of the song, often sung by the vocalist(s) or played by the main instrument.
pg090_n0018: It is usually the part that people hum or sing along to.
pg090_n0019: A strong melody is memorable and catchy, making it a crucial part of songwriting.
pg090_n0023: Lyrics: These are words of a song that express emotions, tell a story or convey a message.
pg090_n0024: Good lyrics often have a strong theme, clear structure, and impactful wording that connects with the audience.
pg090_n0028: Harmony: This refers to the vocals and background music that support the melody.
pg090_n0029: Harmony adds depth and emotion to a song and is created through voices and instruments such as guitar, piano and others.
pg090_n0033: Rhythm: This includes the beats and tempo of the song that determine its energy and pace.
pg090_n0034: A song’s rhythm can be slow and emotional, creating a calmness.
pg090_n0035: It can also be fast and energetic, making a song exciting and lively.
pg090_n0036: In some songs, a rhythm can be moderate (that is, between slow and fast), depending on the mood the composer wants to create.
pg090_n0040: Song structure: A well-composed song falls under a particular structure.
pg090_n0041: For instance, most popular songs in genres such as Bongo fleva, Hip hop, R&B and others follow a standard format which is verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus.
pg090_n0042: A verse introduces the theme or story of the song, a chorus is the most memorable and repeated section, often carrying the main message, while a bridge is a different section that adds variation in the song and leads back to the chorus.
pg090_n0043: Note that song structures differ depending on the genre and choices of the composer.

pg091_n0047: Songwriting is a creative activity that combines inspiration, feelings and musical skills to make songs that connect with people.
pg091_n0048: Understanding the essential steps in writing a song can make the process clearer and more organised.
pg092_n0002: is important in turning a simple idea into a complete and well-made song.
pg092_n0003: The following are the essential processes involved in songwriting:
pg092_n0005: (a) Finding inspiration: The first step in a songwriting is finding inspiration.
pg092_n0006: Inspiration can come from personal experiences, emotions, nature, books or even other songs.
pg092_n0007: Many songwriters start by jotting down ideas or recording melodies that come to mind.
pg092_n0009: (b) Choosing the song structure: A well-structured song has different sections, including the verse, chorus and bridge.
pg092_n0010: The right time to decide on the structure of a song depends on the songwriter’s creative process.
pg092_n0011: Some songwriters establish the structure early, especially if they follow a common format like verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus.
pg092_n0012: Others allow the song to evolve naturally, shaping the structure after developing the melody or lyrics.
pg092_n0014: (c) Creating the melody: Once an idea is formed and the song structure is identified, the next step is to create the melody.
pg092_n0015: The melody should be catchy, memorable and reflect the song’s mood.
pg092_n0016: Before deciding on the most suitable melody for the song, composers often try out various notes and rhythms.
pg092_n0017: Playing an instrument like a guitar or piano can help in creating the melody.
pg092_n0018: At this stage, the composer can develop a melody for a verse, chorus and bridge.
pg092_n0020: (d) Writing the lyrics: Lyrics are important for telling a story, expressing emotions or conveying a particular message through the song.
pg092_n0021: Some composers start with lyrics before composing a melody, while others fit the lyrics into the existing melody.
pg092_n0022: In our case, since we already have the melody, this stage will involve preparing the lyrics and fitting them into the existing melody.
pg092_n0023: Composers often rewrite lyrics multiple times to ensure they fit well with the melody and maintain a smooth flow.
pg092_n0025: (e) Arranging the song: After composing the melody and lyrics, the next step is arranging the song.
pg092_n0026: This involves deciding which instruments will be used and how different sections will be played.
pg092_n0027: At this stage, a songwriter may get assistance from a producer or song arranger.
pg092_n0029: (f) Refining and finalising the song: At this stage, songwriters review and refine their work, making changes to improve the song’s structure, melody or lyrics.
pg092_n0030: They listen to the song multiple times to identify areas that need adjustment.
pg092_n0031: Some songs go through multiple drafts before they are finalised.
pg092_n0032: After the song is refined, a songwriter may perform the song live or work in a studio for professional production.

pg093_n0033: Ensemble performances in music involve a group of musicians playing instruments or singing together to create a unified sound.
pg093_n0034: These performances can range from small to large groups of musicians.
pg093_n0035: A good ensemble performance depends on balance, teamwork, and communication between the musicians.
pg093_n0036: Furthermore, ensemble performances often require strong leadership, whether
pg094_n0002: from a conductor in larger groups or through shared leadership in smaller groups.
pg094_n0003: Performing in an ensemble helps musicians develop skills like cooperation, discipline and creativity.
pg094_n0007: Vocal ensemble performances are an important part of music, bringing together multiple singers to create a rich and harmonious sound.
pg094_n0008: Singing in an ensemble requires teamwork since singers must blend their voices, stay in tune, and keep the rhythm together to create a smooth and unified sound.
pg094_n0009: Different cultures have their own unique traditions of vocal ensemble singing, with special techniques and styles that make each performance different.
pg094_n0010: In different societies, vocal ensemble performances are a powerful way to tell stories, express emotions, and bring people together through music.
pg094_n0012: Principles of singing in a vocal ensemble
pg094_n0016: Understanding each part of the song to be sung:
pg094_n0017: An ensemble singer should understand each part of the song before the performance.
pg094_n0018: Apart from participating in ensemble rehearsals, individual singers can go through the tune, words, musical terms and signs, and other parts of the song over and over on their own time before getting to the performance.
pg094_n0019: This will increase confidence to singers and make them have good performance.
pg094_n0023: This simply means to accurately sing the correct notes of a musical piece.
pg094_n0024: When singing in an ensemble, it is important for all singers to sing in tune to produce sounds that are in agreement.
pg094_n0025: Proper voice production will enable a singer to sing in tune.
pg094_n0028: Singing while carefully listening to each other:
pg094_n0029: This guides singers to avoid singing differently from others.
pg094_n0030: It ensures that no singer in an ensemble is either louder or softer than others.
pg094_n0031: It also helps to make sure that no one is in a different tune or tempo.
pg094_n0032: This will make the voices of the whole ensemble blend well and sound pleasantly.
pg094_n0035: Paying a close attention to the conductor and follow the instructions:
pg094_n0036: During performance in an ensemble, singers should always keep their eyes to the conductor to receive various instructions and respond together as a team.
pg094_n0037: For example, the conductor will give a sign when to start or end a song, or will do any action based on the song message being communicated to the audience.
pg094_n0038: A singer who may go astray during performance can adjust oneself by paying attention to the conductor.
pg095_n0002: (e) Observing correct timing: To achieve this, singers should accurately observe the rhythm of the song so as to sing with correct timing.
pg095_n0003: They should also carefully follow the ensemble conductor to align with the tempo of the song.
pg095_n0005: (f) Proper breath control: Proper breath control is very essential in a vocal ensemble as it helps singers sustain notes and finish song phrases at the right time with the right sound.
pg095_n0006: Correct body posture during singing enhances breath control.
pg095_n0008: (g) Correct diction and articulation: Singers must observe correct pronunciation of words and articulation of consonants and vowels while singing.
pg095_n0009: This ensures that the lyrics are well heard by the audience, hence the message of the song is well understood.
pg095_n0015: In a group, sing a short musical piece at different tempos, following a metronome or conductor.
pg095_n0016: Make sure to sing together to match the tempo precisely.
pg095_n0018: Arrangement of singers for a vocal ensemble
pg095_n0020: When performing in a vocal ensemble, it is important for singers to properly arrange themselves in a specific formation on the stage to create a good performance.
pg095_n0021: The decision on formation can be determined by several criteria, including the total number of singers in the group.
pg095_n0022: For example, one of the most preferred formations in vocal choir ensembles is “curved rows”.
pg095_n0023: This allows those at the ends to sing towards each other, and easily hear those on the other side of the group.
pg095_n0024: It also allows the conductor to easily see and hear everyone in the choir.
pg095_n0025: In curved rows, singers can be arranged by voice; that is, soprano, alto, tenor and bass.
pg095_n0026: For example, for a small choir of twelve singers, they can be arranged in just one row.
pg095_n0027: Sopranos will be positioned on the left.
pg095_n0028: Moving to the right, follows the altos, the tenors and finally, the basses.
pg095_n0029: Three members of each voice will be placed in the row.

pg097_n0031: Singers and instrumentalists create an exciting and powerful musical experience through vocal-instrumental ensemble performances.
pg097_n0032: These performances can be small, like a few singers with a piano, or large, like a choir with multiple musical
pg098_n0003: The combination of voices and instruments adds depth to the music, making it alive and more emotional.
pg098_n0004: Throughout history, vocal-instrumental ensembles have been important in many musical styles, including church music, Jazz, Pop, Taarab, Muziki wa dansi, Bongo fleva and others.
pg098_n0005: These performances also reflect different cultures and historical periods, showing how music changes over time.
pg098_n0006: To create a balanced sound, composers and arrangers carefully design how the voices and instruments work together so that no part is too loud or too soft.
pg098_n0008: Essential techniques for a vocal-instrumental ensemble
pg098_n0010: A successful performance in a vocal-instrumental ensemble is not just about having good singers and instrument players.
pg098_n0011: It is about working together as a team with great coordination, balance and musical awareness.
pg098_n0012: Singers and instrument players must listen to each other and stay in one page.
pg098_n0013: The following are essential techniques for performers in a vocal-instrumental ensemble to consider to create music that sounds clear, exciting and well-coordinated.
pg098_n0017: A well-balanced and blend between instruments and voices:
pg098_n0018: In a vocal-instrumental ensemble, the voices and instruments should complement each other, not overpower.
pg098_n0019: Singers must match their volume with the instruments.
pg098_n0020: As well, instrument players should adjust their playing to support the vocals.
pg098_n0024: Strong communication between singers and instrumentalists ensures that the performance stays coordinated.
pg098_n0025: Eye contact and body language between them help coordinate signs, entrances and changes in music.
pg098_n0026: Performers should also pay attention to the conductor or band leader as he or she plays a crucial role in guiding tempo, dynamics and changes in music.
pg098_n0030: Everyone should stay on the beat to avoid sounding disordered.
pg098_n0031: Singers and instrument players must count the beats to enter their parts at the right time.
pg098_n0032: In a vocal-instrumental ensemble, performers are encouraged to have enough practice before a performance.
pg098_n0033: This helps them develop a strong sense of timing and ensures smooth transitions during performance.
pg098_n0037: Changing volume levels through musical dynamics makes the performance more interesting and emotional.
pg098_n0038: For example, singing or playing softly can create a calm or intimate feeling, while louder sections of a song add excitement and energy.
pg098_n0039: Singers can also use changes in tone,
pg099_n0002: facial expressions, and body language to express emotions and bring the song to life.
pg099_n0003: On the other hand, musicians can match the mood of the lyrics by adjusting their playing style.
pg099_n0004: For example, a gentle piano melody can make a sad song more touching, while strong drum beats can add power to a cheerful song.
pg099_n0007: In a vocal-instrumental ensemble, singers and instrument players must listen carefully to each other to maintain a balance and harmony.
pg099_n0008: If an instrument or voice is too loud, quick adjustments should be made rather than competing for attention.
pg099_n0009: This technique ensures that all singers and instruments stay in the key.
pg099_n0012: Stage presence is the ability of a performer to capture and hold the audience’s attention through his or her confidence, energy and engagement.
pg099_n0013: It involves body language, facial expressions, movement, and interaction with the audience to make the performance more engaging and memorable.
pg099_n0014: In a vocal-instrumental ensemble, performers should maintain good posture, use expressive body language and avoid looking stiff or disengaged.
pg099_n0015: A perfect stage presence and confidence come from thorough preparation before the performance.

pg100_n0030: A piano is a large keyboard musical instrument with a wooden case enclosing a sound board.
pg100_n0031: It has strings that sound when struck by hammers operated from a keyboard.
pg100_n0032: The standard modern piano has 88 buttons, commonly named keys, with a range of seven full octaves plus some few keys.
pg101_n0004: It is important to know different parts of the piano and their functions.
pg101_n0005: Knowledge about the parts and functions helps to understand how the piano works and how to play it well.
pg101_n0006: Each part of the piano plays a special role in making music.
pg101_n0007: The main parts of the piano include the following:
pg101_n0011: Keyboard: A board with black and white keys that produce different tones when pressed.
pg101_n0014: The fallboard: It is the part of a piano that usually folds down over the keys to cover and protect the keyboard when the piano is not in use.
pg101_n0015: It keeps the keys safe from dust, dirt and accidental damage.
pg101_n0018: The piano lid: The top cover of the piano that can be opened to increase sound projection or closed to protect the instrument.
pg101_n0021: Music rack: It holds sheet music or books in place so that the pianist can read and play at the same time.
pg101_n0022: It is usually located just above the keyboard and can often be adjusted or folded down when not in use.
pg101_n0025: Pedals: They are found at the bottom of the piano.
pg101_n0026: They help control the length and quality of the sound.
pg101_n0027: The right pedal (sustain pedal) makes the notes keep sounding even after the player lifts his or her fingers from the keys.
pg101_n0028: This helps the music sound smooth and connected.
pg101_n0029: The middle pedal (sostenuto pedal) holds only the notes that are being played when the pedal is pressed, while other notes played later will not be sustained.
pg101_n0030: The left pedal (soft pedal) makes the sound softer and gentler.
pg101_n0033: Strings and hammers: These are found inside the piano.
pg101_n0034: When the keys are pressed, the harmers strike the strings to produce sound.

pg102_n0022: Names of the keys on the piano keyboard
pg102_n0024: The piano keys are named using the first seven letters of the alphabets which are A, B, C, D, E, F and G.
pg102_n0025: A complete piano keyboard has 88 keys.
pg102_n0026: These are categorised into 52 white keys and 36 black keys.
pg102_n0027: Black keys are also called enharmonic keys because every black key has two names derived from two white keys on its left and right sides.
pg102_n0028: Thus, a black key can either be flat or sharp.
pg102_n0029: For example, a black key named as “A” sharp (A♯) is also a B flat (B♭).

pg103_n0009: Having the correct posture is very important when playing the piano.
pg103_n0010: It helps the pianist play comfortably and avoid injury or tiredness.
pg103_n0011: The following are some guidelines for a correct posture when playing a piano:
pg103_n0015: Positioning at the middle of the piano, that is, in front of middle C.
pg103_n0016: This will also depend on the piece of music being played.
pg103_n0017: If the musical piece uses only the upper or lower part of the piano, the player should adjust the sitting position to the required part of the piano.
pg103_n0020: Sitting on the front half of the seat.
pg103_n0021: This posture enables the player to easily move the feet when playing the piano pedals.
pg103_n0024: Releasing and relaxing the feet while keeping them horizontal on the ground from the heel to toe, and ready to move when using the pedals.
pg103_n0027: Releasing and relaxing the shoulders and arms.
pg103_n0033: Playing the piano while placing the fingers in a curved position to make it easier to press the keys smoothly.

pg108_n0003: Playing major scales on the piano
pg108_n0005: Playing major scales on the piano is an important skill for learning music.
pg108_n0006: It normally follows a pattern of whole and half steps that form a major scale.
pg108_n0007: To play major scales, pianists must understand the correct fingering for each scale to play smoothly and quickly.

pg114_n0022: The ‘A’ minor scale is relative to the C major scale.
pg114_n0023: Thus, both the ‘A’ minor and C major scales share a key signature.
pg114_n0024: Therefore, like the C major scale, ‘A’ natural minor scale involves only white keys on a piano but starts on note A.
pg114_n0025: When playing ‘A’ natural minor scale, the fingering is the same as in C major scale.
pg114_n0026: However, when playing ‘A’ harmonic minor scale, note G becomes G♯.

pg117_n0014: Triads can be grouped into primary and secondary ones.
pg117_n0015: In this section, you will learn how to play primary triads on the piano in C, G and F major keys.
pg117_n0016: In a scale, primary triads are built on the 1st (tonic), 4th and 5th degrees.
pg117_n0017: For example, in the C major scale, the primary triads are built on notes C, F and G.
pg117_n0018: In written music, a triad built on the 1st (tonic) note of the scale is labelled as I, on the 4th note as IV and on the 5th note as V.
pg117_n0019: On the piano, primary triads are played using the 1st, 3rd and 5th fingers of the right hand and the 5th, 3rd and 1st fingers of the left hand.
pg117_n0021: Playing primary triads in C major scale
pg117_n0023: Since primary triads are built on the 1st (tonic), 4th and 5th degrees of a scale, in the C major scale, the primary triads will be C E G, F A C and G B D.
pg117_n0024: Triad C E G also known as the tonic triad, is built on the 1st (tonic) note of the scale which is C, triad F A C is built on the 4th note of the scale which is F, while triad G B D is built on the 5th note which is G.

pg125_n0008: Music production is now becoming a major career for many Tanzanian youths.
pg125_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of music production, the structure of a music recording studio, basic stages of the music production process and job opportunities related to music production.
pg125_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to describe the main parts of a music recording studio and recognise the purpose of common studio equipment and tools.
pg125_n0011: You will also be able to plan simple music production sessions and assess personal interests and talents in relation to music production careers.
pg125_n0019: Music production is a process in which music is created, recorded and preserved to be distributed to the users.
pg125_n0020: The produced music can either be instrumental, vocal or both.
pg125_n0021: In music production, producers employ technology to capture and process musical sounds to produce the desired music.
pg125_n0022: The process of music production can either be done in a music studio or a live performance setting.
pg125_n0023: At this level, you will learn about studio music production.
pg125_n0027: A music recording studio is a special room where music and other sounds are recorded.
pg125_n0028: It is carefully built to make sure that the sound is clear and of good
pg126_n0003: A music studio has special equipment that help to record, mix and improve the sound before it is shared with the audience.
pg126_n0004: People go to a music recording studio to record songs, instrumental music or even spoken words.
pg126_n0005: A music recording studio usually has two main rooms, namely, the control room and the live room.
pg126_n0009: This is the room where a music producer works.
pg126_n0010: Music producers guide the process of producing music.
pg126_n0011: They may produce music for singers, rappers or instrumentalists.
pg126_n0012: They may also produce music for movies and design sounds for video games.
pg126_n0013: In the control room, there are recording equipment and tools that the producer uses to record and control the music.
pg126_n0014: In this room, the producer listens carefully to the sound, change things like volume and balance, and make sure everything sounds good.
pg126_n0015: The control room is a quiet space, and it is built in a way that helps the producer hear the sound clearly.
pg126_n0016: Figures 7.1 shows an example of the control room.
pg126_im003: Control room of a music recording studio with a computer, mixing console and keyboard, studio monitor speakers, headphones, soundproof wall panels, and a large window into the recording room.
pg126_n0018: Figure 7.1: The control room in a music recording studio
pg126_n0022: This is where the singers, instrumentalists or speakers perform.
pg126_n0023: They sing, play instruments or talk while the producer records them.
pg127_n0002: to stop unwanted sounds, like echoes or noise from outside, so the recording is clean and clear.
pg127_n0003: Sometimes, more than one person can perform in the live room at the same time.
pg127_n0004: Figure 7.2 shows an example of the live room in a music recording studio.

pg127_n0008: Note that, there is usually a large glass window between the control room and the live room.
pg127_n0009: This window lets the producer see the performers and also helps with communication.
pg127_n0010: The producer can give signs or instructions while the recording is happening.

pg128_n0005: Acoustic treatment in a music recording studio
pg128_n0007: Acoustic treatment is the control of echoes and unwanted noise in a recording studio.
pg128_n0008: When someone sings or plays an instrument in a studio, the sound bounces off the walls, floor and ceiling.
pg128_n0009: These bouncing sounds are called echoes.
pg128_n0010: If the microphone picks up these echoes, the recording will not sound natural.
pg128_n0011: It may sound blurry or messy.
pg128_n0012: Every music recording studio needs acoustic treatment to produce high-quality music.
pg128_n0014: There are various methods of acoustic treatment that can be applied to prevent echoes from getting into the microphone.
pg128_n0015: One of the common methods is the use of foam panels.
pg128_n0016: This is a special soft foam placed on the walls to absorb sound and stop echoes from bouncing around the room.
pg128_n0017: Another method is the use of a thick wool carpet on the floor to soak up sound.
pg128_n0018: A thick wool carpet also stops the sound from bouncing off the hard floor.

pg129_n0018: Several equipment and tools are required for music to be produced.
pg129_n0019: The following are some of the basic equipment and tools used in music production:
pg129_n0021: (a) Computer: This is a device into which specific software for music production is installed.
pg129_n0022: After installing the software, a music producer can use the computer to edit, mix and master recorded music.

pg129_n0027: (b) Keyboard MIDI controller: The term ‘MIDI’ stands for Musical Instrument Digital Interface.
pg129_n0028: A keyboard MIDI controller does not usually create or produce sound by itself without being connected to the computer.
pg129_n0029: When it is connected to a computer, the keys can be played, and the computer will convert what is played into sound.

pg130_n0006: A studio microphone is a device which captures the sound that is being recorded.
pg130_n0007: The sound can be a vocal or a played musical instrument such as a guitar, zeze or any other instrument.
pg130_n0008: Figure 7.6 shows an example of a studio microphone.
pg130_im004: Studio condenser microphone with a metal mesh grille and gold-colored body.
pg130_n0014: Studio monitors are a pair of speakers used for listening to the music during the recording, mixing and mastering processes.
pg130_n0015: They can also be found in radio and television studios.
pg130_n0016: Studio monitors can be placed on a table or a stand.
pg130_n0017: Figure 7.7 shows an example of a pair of studio monitors placed on stands.

pg131_n0002: Figure 7.7: Studio monitors placed on stands
pg131_n0006: An audio interface, also known as a sound card, is a device that allows the transfer of sound to and from the computer.
pg131_n0007: Microphone, MIDI controller, studio monitors and instruments such as guitars and others are connected to the audio interface.
pg131_n0008: Figure 7.8 shows an example of an audio interface.
pg131_im004: A red audio interface with four input ports, gain knobs, and headphone and monitor controls on the front panel.
pg131_n0014: This is an electronic device which combines the sounds of different audio signals.
pg131_n0015: These audio signals may be of either a singer, musical instruments or both, picked up by a microphone or cable connected to an audio mixer.
pg131_n0016: Figure 7.9 shows an example of an audio mixer.

pg132_n0003: This is a pair of earphones worn over the head when listening to the music which is being produced.
pg132_n0004: A singer can wear headphones to listen to the instrumental music when recording a song.
pg132_n0005: A producer or studio technician can also use headphones to listen to the music they are producing.
pg132_n0006: Good quality headphones help a producer or studio technician to hear how the final audio will sound.

pg132_n0012: A pop filter is an equipment designed to reduce the popping sounds before they reach the microphone.
pg132_n0013: When singing into a microphone, your mouth can produce popping sounds when producing sounds such as “p” or “b”.
pg132_n0014: In most cases, these sounds are unpleasant and unwanted in a recorded song.

pg133_n0004: It allows the microphone to be positioned in the studio without requiring a person to hold it.

pg134_n0059: Basic stages of the music production process
pg134_n0061: There are several stages that a producer follows in music production.
pg134_n0062: The following are key stages that can be followed when producing a song:
pg134_n0064: (a) Creating a musical idea: This is the initial stage in which the song’s concept is developed.
pg134_n0065: It involves writing a song and getting it ready for recording.
pg134_n0066: It is also possible for a producer to create instrumental music and give it to a singer(s) to sing along to.
pg134_n0068: (b) Rehearsing the singer(s) on the prepared instrumental music: At this stage, the producer works with the singer(s) to rehearse using the instrumental track that was created.
pg134_n0069: Rehearsals help the performers become familiar with the music and understand how to deliver their vocals effectively during recording.
pg134_n0070: This also helps in identifying areas for improvement before the actual recording begins.
pg135_n0002: (c) Recording: This is the stage where the actual sound is captured.
pg135_n0003: Vocals and instruments are recorded separately or together, depending on the music style and preferences of the producer.
pg135_n0004: This is one of the most critical stages in the music production process, as it forms the base of the final product.
pg135_n0006: (d) Editing: During this stage, the producer makes necessary changes to the recorded tracks.
pg135_n0007: This may include adjusting, cutting, adding or removing certain parts to improve the structure and clarity of the song.
pg135_n0008: The goal is to make the song clean and more pleasant to listen to.
pg135_n0010: (e) Mixing: During the mixing stage, different parts of the recorded vocals and instruments are combined.
pg135_n0011: At this stage, the producer adjusts the volume, adds various sound effects and makes sure everything sounds good together.
pg135_n0013: (f) Mastering: This is the final stage of music production.
pg135_n0014: It is the stage where adjustments are made to the mixed song to achieve maximum sound quality across different listening environments.
pg135_n0015: The song is polished, its volume is adjusted and the sound is improved to make it suitable for distribution.
pg135_n0016: After mastering, the song is ready to be shared through various media outlets such as radio and television stations or the Internet.
pg135_n0018: Job opportunities related to music production
pg135_n0020: Music is a fast-growing industry in Tanzania.
pg135_n0021: Many young people are becoming involved in music as a way to earn a living and build careers.
pg135_n0022: There are many job opportunities related to music production that allow people to work in a music studio or in other parts of the creative industry.
pg135_n0023: These jobs require different skills, talents and training.
pg135_n0024: The following are some examples of job opportunities in the field of music production:
pg135_n0026: (a) Music producer: A music producer is in charge of the process of making songs or albums.
pg135_n0027: They help artists to come up with music ideas, choose which songs to record, and suggest who to work with.
pg135_n0028: Producers also lead the recording sessions and makes sure the music sounds good and meets a high standard.
pg135_n0029: They often use studio equipment and software to create, mix and master the songs.
pg135_n0031: (b) Studio manager: A studio manager is responsible for the daily running of the studio.
pg135_n0032: This person organises bookings for artists and producers, hires studio staff and makes sure all equipment are working properly.
pg136_n0002: also takes part in promoting the studio and attracting new clients, including musicians, advertisers and filmmakers.
pg136_n0005: An audio technician or sound engineer works to make sure that the sound quality is clear and balanced.
pg136_n0006: They operate studio equipment during recordings, do sound checks before sessions and mix and edit the audio after recording.
pg136_n0007: Their role is very important in producing music that sounds professional.
pg136_n0010: A lyricist writes the words (lyrics) to songs.
pg136_n0011: Sometimes, they work alone, and other times they work with musicians or composers.
pg136_n0012: Lyricists help to create meaningful messages in songs by choosing the right words that match the mood and rhythm of the music.
pg136_n0015: A music production teacher is someone who teaches students how to create, record and produce music.
pg136_n0016: They may work in schools, colleges or universities.
pg136_n0017: This job requires good knowledge of music, studio equipment and teaching skills to help learners understand the music production process.
pg136_n0020: A sound designer creates sound effects and audio features for different types of media.
pg136_n0021: These include video games, films, theatre, radio shows and adverts.
pg136_n0022: Sound designers use computers and special equipment to make sure the sound supports the story or message being told.
pg136_n0025: A songwriter is someone who writes songs, often for other people to sing.
pg136_n0026: Many famous songs have been performed by singers who did not write them.
pg136_n0027: In Tanzania, for example, the national anthem and patriotic songs like “Tanzania Nakupenda,” and “Tazama Ramani” have been recorded by many artists who are not the original composers.
pg136_n0028: Songwriting is a creative job that can bring income through music studios, performances and royalties.
pg136_n0031: An instrumentalist is someone who plays a musical instrument.
pg136_n0032: They can record instrumental music and sell it to singers or producers.
pg136_n0033: Instrumentalists are also hired to play their instruments during studio recording sessions.
pg136_n0034: Their work brings richness to recorded songs.

pg007_n0007_easy_read:
Without precise rhythm, music has no clear order.
Then there is nothing to dance to or nod along with.
pg007_n0008_easy_read:
Other parts of music are also important, such as:
- pitch
- dynamics
- harmony
But music cannot exist without rhythm.
pg007_n0009_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn ideas about rhythm.
These ideas include:
- triplets
- time signatures
- grouping notes and rests
pg007_n0010_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- read rhythmic patterns correctly
- write rhythmic patterns correctly
- perform music in different meters
pg007_n0018_easy_read:
A triplet is a group of 3 equal parts.
It happens when a note that is usually divided into 2 equal parts is divided into 3 equal parts instead.
pg007_n0019_easy_read: For example, 1 semibreve can be divided into 3 equal minims.
pg007_n0020_easy_read: A minim can be divided into 3 equal crotchets.
pg007_n0021_easy_read: A crotchet can also be divided into 3 equal quavers.
pg007_n0022_easy_read: Table 1.1 shows how a beat that is usually divided into 2 parts can be divided into 3 equal parts.
pg007_n0023_easy_read:
When you form a triplet, notes with flags are beamed together.
These notes include:
- quavers
- semiquavers
- other smaller notes
The number "3" is placed in the middle of the notes.
pg007_n0024_easy_read:
Notes without flags, such as crotchets and minims, are grouped with a straight or curved line.
The number "3" is placed in the middle.

You can also count triplets while you clap.
You can use numbers or syllables, like with other notes.
pg008_n0033_easy_read:
When you count the beats with numbers, add the word ‘triplet’ or the syllables ‘la’ and ‘li’ after the number.
See figures 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3.

pg012_n0016_easy_read:
Time signatures in music are an important part of rhythm.
They help musicians understand how beats are grouped in a piece.
pg012_n0017_easy_read:
They show:
- the number of beats in each measure
- which note gets 1 beat
pg012_n0018_easy_read: When a musician understands how time signatures change the feel of a piece of music, the musician can interpret and perform the music well.
pg012_n0022_easy_read: In simple time signatures, each beat can be divided into 2 equal parts.
pg012_n0023_easy_read:
These are called "simple" because each beat divides naturally into 2 parts.
This makes them easy to count and play.
pg012_n0024_easy_read:
In this section, you will learn about these simple time signatures:
- two-two
- three-two
- four-two
- three-eight
pg013_n0002_easy_read:
A 2/2 time signature:
People also write this with the symbol called alla breve or cut-time.
pg013_n0003_easy_read: A 2/2 time signature means there are 2 minims in 1 bar.
pg013_n0004_easy_read: In 2/2 time, 1 beat has the value of a minim.
pg013_n0005_easy_read: Figures 1.11 to 1.13 show examples of rhythms in 2/2 time.
pg013_n0013_easy_read:
A 3/2 time signature:
This time signature shows that there are 3 minims in 1 bar.
pg013_n0014_easy_read: In 3/2 time, 1 beat also has the value of a minim.
pg013_n0015_easy_read: Figures 1.14 and 1.15 show examples of rhythms in 3/2 time.
pg013_n0021_easy_read:
A 4/2 time signature:
This time signature shows that there are 4 minims in 1 bar.
pg013_n0022_easy_read: In 4/2 time, 1 beat has the value of a minim too.
pg013_n0023_easy_read: Figures 1.16 and 1.17 show examples of rhythms in 4/2 time.
pg014_n0006_easy_read: A 3/8 time signature: This time signature shows that there are 3 quavers in 1 bar.
pg014_n0007_easy_read: In 3/8 time, 1 beat has the value of a quaver.
pg014_n0008_easy_read: Figures 1.18 and 1.19 show examples of rhythms in 3/8 time.
pg014_n0016_easy_read:
You can count and clap rhythms in different simple time signatures.
You can use numbers or syllables.

pg018_n0019_easy_read: Note grouping means arranging notes and rests to match the time signature.
pg018_n0020_easy_read: It means joining notes into groups with beams, or arranging notes and rests correctly to match the time signature used.
pg018_n0021_easy_read: Note grouping is important in music because it makes written music easier to read.
pg018_n0025_easy_read: These are rules that help musicians group notes so the music is easier to read and play.
pg018_n0026_easy_read: These rules depend on the time signature. The time signature shows how many beats are in each measure and how the beats are divided.
pg018_n0027_easy_read: When notes are grouped correctly, it is easier to see where each beat is and how the rhythm moves.
pg018_n0028_easy_read: This helps the person writing the music and the person playing the music understand the music better.
pg018_n0029_easy_read: Here are some rules for grouping notes in music writing:
pg018_n0031_easy_read:
(a) Do not beam across a bar line.
Beaming happens inside the measure.
pg018_n0032_easy_read: If a note stands alone at the end of a measure, it should not be
pg019_n0002_easy_read: Connect it to the first beat of the next measure.
pg019_n0003_easy_read: Figure 1.30 shows how to avoid beaming across a bar line.
pg019_n0012_easy_read: Figure 1.30: How to avoid beaming across a bar line
pg019_n0014_easy_read: (b) Do not beam across the centre of a measure:
pg019_n0015_easy_read: For example, in 4/4 time signatures, the centre of the measure is between the 2nd and 3rd beats.
pg019_n0016_easy_read: The 2 beats are always separate. This makes the rhythm clear for the reader.
pg019_n0017_easy_read: Figure 1.31 shows how to avoid beaming across the centre of a measure.
pg019_n0026_easy_read: Figure 1.31: How to avoid beaming across the centre of a measure
pg019_n0028_easy_read: (c) Check the total number of semiquavers to group:
pg019_n0029_easy_read: Usually, in a time signature where a crotchet is the main beat, you can group a maximum of 4 semiquavers together.
pg019_n0030_easy_read: Figure 1.32 shows the grouping of semiquavers in 4/4 time.
pg019_n0033_easy_read: Figure 1.32: Grouping of semiquavers in 4/4 time
pg019_n0035_easy_read: (d) Note grouping includes beaming notes that belong to the same beat.
pg019_n0036_easy_read: However, this rule does not apply to all time signatures.
pg019_n0037_easy_read: For example, in 3/8 and 4/4 time, notes that do not belong to the same beat can be beamed.
pg019_n0038_easy_read: In 3/8 time, it is acceptable to beam 3 quavers or 6 semiquavers, as Figure 1.33 shows.
pg020_n0002_easy_read: Figure 1.33: Beaming quavers and semiquavers in 3-8 time
pg020_n0004_easy_read: In 4-4 time, you can beam 4 quavers in the first minim beat or the second minim beat, as shown in figures 1.34 and 1.35.
pg020_n0008_easy_read: Figure 1.35: Beaming quavers and semiquavers in 4-4 time

pg020_n0012_easy_read: This means how notes are arranged by sight and rhythm inside measures, based on the time signature of a piece.
pg020_n0013_easy_read: In each time signature, notes are grouped to show the strong beats and the weak beats clearly.
pg020_n0014_easy_read:
Correct note grouping for each time signature helps musicians:
- understand the rhythm more easily
- match the style or mood of the music
- keep the written music clear and organised

pg023_n0017_easy_read:
In music, group notes and rests by the time signature.
This makes the rhythm clear and organised.
pg023_n0018_easy_read: Grouping helps performers understand the timing and stress of each beat in a measure.
pg023_n0019_easy_read: However, you must follow some rules when you group notes and rests in measures.
pg023_n0022_easy_read: (a) Group notes and rests by the division of the beat:
pg023_n0023_easy_read: When you use rests in a bar, the rests must show the main beat of the time signature.
pg023_n0024_easy_read: Figures 1.45 and 1.46 show the correct and incorrect ways for rests to show the main beat.
